blocks.text: Where the North Bound Specification defines the protocol and data-model contract RDK-B exposes upward to the operator and cloud, the South Bound Specification covers the other direction: the contract between RDK-B middleware and the silicon/BSP underneath it. This is the surface a SoC or vendor team implements against to bring a new platform up on RDK-B.
In practice this surface isn't a single uniform API. Two distinct patterns exist side by side across RDK-B components, and both are in scope for this page.

Formal HAL interfaces: a defined header (the rdkb-halif-* repos) that a vendor implements for their chipset — Wi-Fi, Cable Modem, GPON, xDSL, Ethernet Switch, MoCA, Cellular, Platform, Voice, and others. This is the traditional RDK Ready certification surface.

OSS southbound delegation: several "manager" components (WAN Manager, DHCP Manager, XDNS, Utopia's DHCP server path, and others) don't implement their protocol themselves — they orchestrate an existing open-source tool (pppd, udhcpc, dnsmasq, iproute2, ipset, libnl, wireless-tools, and similar) via config files, system calls, or netlink, and report status back up through the data model. There's no vendor-implemented header here; the "southbound" dependency is on the OSS package itself, not a chipset contract.
This page, and the List of South Bound APIs it links to, cover:
Every RDK-B-defined HAL interface tracked in hal-repos.json, each backed by its own rdkb-halif-* repo and versioned header.

The OSS packages and system-level utilities RDK-B components delegate to instead of a formal HAL, where that delegation has been verified against real component source or official RDK documentation (not inferred from naming).
Out of scope: the North Bound data model those components expose (see the North Bound Specification), and internal component-to-component IPC (RBUS, sysevent), which isn't a vendor-facing boundary.

HAL Interface: A versioned header file defining the function calls, structs, and enums a vendor implements to bridge an RDK-B component to their chipset or BSP. Published as its own rdkb-halif-* repo.
Vendor Implementation: The vendor's own closed- or open-source code behind a HAL interface header, built and linked against the platform's SDK. Not published in the rdkb-halif-* repo itself.

OSS Southbound Delegation: The pattern where an RDK-B "manager" component (e.g. WAN Manager, DHCP Manager) doesn't own a protocol implementation itself, but configures and monitors a general-purpose open-source package (dnsmasq, pppd, udhcpc, iproute2, and similar) that does the real work. No vendor-specific header is involved; every platform runs the same upstream package.

RDK Ready Certification: A per-HAL-interface test and certification program. Because certification is modular, a Wi-Fi SoC vendor certifies only against the RDK-B Wi-Fi HAL, a DOCSIS SoC vendor only against the Cable Modem HAL — allowing operators to mix vendors across subsystems on the same platform.
Formal HAL interfaces (rdkb-halif-*)
Broadband access & connectivity: Cable Modem HAL, GPON HAL, EPON HAL, xDSL HAL, Ethernet Switch HAL, WiFi HAL, MoCA HAL, Cellular HAL, Cellular Modem HAL, WAN HAL, VLAN HAL, Bridge Utility HAL.
Platform & lifecycle: Platform HAL, Firmware Upgrade HAL, eMMC HAL, DHCP HAL, DHCPv6 Client HAL, Direct Kernel Access.
Voice & apps: MTA (Voice Gateway) HAL, Voice HAL, LPA (eSIM) HAL, MSO HAL, Bluetooth, Matter, Thread, Zigbee, Container.
OSS southbound delegation (no vendor header — same upstream package on every platform)

WAN/network stack: PPPD, DHCPv6 client tooling (dibbler-client, dibbler-server, ti_udhcpc, udhcpc), Dnsmasq, Firewall-Iptables, UPNP, iproute2, ipset, zebra, libnl, libnetfilter_conntrack, net-tools, procps, bridge-utils, wireless-tools.
Wi-Fi tooling adjacent to the WiFi HAL: libhostap, wlancfg, wlancfg_tr, mocacfg, mocactl, ivictl.
The full, current list — including which repo and branch backs each entry — is on the List of South Bound APIs page.

Vendor interfaces evolve over time, so each rdkb-halif-* repo, the RDK-B component consuming it, and the vendor code certified against it are kept in version lockstep — a component declares which HAL major/minor version it expects, and certification is tied to that specific version, not just the interface name.

OSS southbound delegation carries a different kind of compatibility concern: because the same upstream package runs unmodified across platforms, the relevant version to track is the package version pinned in the build (e.g. the dnsmasq or pppd release), not a header revision. A behavior change there affects every RDK-B platform using that component, not just one vendor's implementation.
